summary:
Legal gender recognition in Chile rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019. Adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery. People aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and the law does not cover those under 14. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the "over 14 years old" wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, but the ruling applies only to that case.

Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. A bill criminalising incitement to hatred or violence on grounds including sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression passed the Chamber of Deputies on 9 January 2020; its subsequent legislative status is not sourced here. Article 373 of the Penal Code, covering offences to morals and good customs, was historically used by police to harass gay people for holding hands in public. A 2015 Movilh report recorded, for the first time in seven years, no police abuses against LGBT people, credited to the Carabineros Human Rights Department.

Entry and asylum protections are statutory. The Migration and Immigration Law, enacted 11 April 2021, bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that unrecognized asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk because of, among other grounds, sexual orientation or gender identity.

Trans visitors and residents face documented lethal and near-lethal violence. In 2023 Ever, a young trans man, was murdered by an acquaintance who dismembered the body and concealed it for 24 hours; the case is described as Chile's biggest hate crime and the killer confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for nearly an hour in a transphobic attack at a Santiago hotel, with the victim recounting that the attacker said he wanted to kill him.

Institutional discrimination remains documented alongside the protective framework. In April 2025 Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros, alleging she was relegated to administrative work, had her private life exposed without consent, and was denied support. A Chilean advocacy group's annual report judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTQ rights, citing stalled equality and trans-rights legislation, the rise of the ultra-right and government inaction.

Detention carries specific protections. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing trans detainees recognition of their assumed gender, including placement and segmented housing by gender identity, entry examinations, and rules on access for trans visitors, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation. Since 2009 the National Organization of Gendarmeries has ended disciplinary sanctions against inmates that prevented them from dressing according to their gender identity.

Health care is regulated and publicly funded. A 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to call and register transgender people by their social name. Since 2013 sex reassignment surgeries and hormone therapy have been funded by the Fondo Nacional de Salud. In June 2024 the Ministry of Health's Circular 7 suggested deferring initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, though the Medical College noted physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by 7 to 3, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) through the 2026 Budget Law, but the Ministry of Health-run program continues providing support in medical centers. The Gender Identity Support Program Crece con Orgullo has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Education is the most heavily regulated sphere. A Ministry of Education circular of April 2017, Rights of girls, boys and trans students in the field of education, requires schools nationwide to provide bathroom and shower facilities that respect the gender identity of trans students, alongside guarantees of social name use and gender-conforming uniforms, and non-compliance is sanctionable. It sits within the 2009 General Law of Education, the 2011 School Violence Law requiring Good School Coexistence Committees, the 2013 Superintendence of Education handbook on non-discriminatory treatment, the 2015-2018 National School Coexistence Policy incorporating the International Day Against Homosexuality and Transphobia into the 2016 School Calendar, and the School Inclusion law effective March 2016. Law 21,430, published 15 March 2022, is the first regulation explicitly protecting LGBTIQA+ children and adolescents, including non-discrimination on sex characteristics and the right to develop gender identity, and obliges state bodies to create programs on sexual rights and diversity.

Legislative pressure runs against part of this framework. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report by 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation proposing to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors, and repeal Circular 812 protecting gender identity in schools.
tangentialFactors:
Chile's protections were built through sustained domestic campaigning rather than litigation alone. Movilh, the Chilean LGBT integration movement, indexes its milestone wins as the anti-discrimination law, inclusive questions in the 2012 census, the "El amor es amor" marriage campaign, and local-level work under the Comuna Diversa banner with regional branches; it published its 24th Annual Human Rights Report on sexual and gender diversity covering 2025.

Perception data exist but are recorded here only in outline. The F&M Global Barometers country profile for Chile carries composite scores measuring LGBT rights perception, including a specific Global Barometer of Transgender Rights index; the inventory does not report the actual values, so no comparative ranking can be stated.

The documented violence cases differ in profile: the 2023 killing of Ever was carried out by a known acquaintance and concealed, while the 2021 Santiago hotel assault was a group attack on a couple with explicit death threats. Both predate the current legislative period and neither indicates a legal vacuum, since hate-motivated aggravation has applied since 2012.
localsOnly:
Residents have a statutory route to recognition that does not depend on medical evidence: adults apply directly to the Civil Registry under Law 21,120, while 14-to-18-year-olds go before family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents. The April 2025 Constitutional Court decision on the age wording extended relief to one 10-year-old applicant only, so the under-14 pathway otherwise remains closed.

Publicly funded transition care is available through the Fondo Nacional de Salud, which has covered sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013. Ministry of Health programs continue to deliver gender identity support after Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's PAIG in the 2026 Budget Law, and Crece con Orgullo has served ages 3 to 17 since 2023.

Trans students have enforceable rights in schools: bathroom and shower access matching gender identity, social name use, and gender-conforming uniforms under the April 2017 circular, with non-compliance sanctionable, plus the child-rights protections of Law 21,430 and the School Inclusion law. Health facilities are separately required by the 2011 circular to register patients by social name.

In custody, placement, segmented housing, entry examinations and visitor access follow the assumed gender under the Gendarmería protocol, and since 2009 inmates cannot be disciplined for dressing according to their gender identity.

Movement-level records include inclusive 2012 census questions and the Comuna Diversa municipal program, both of which shape how LGBT residents are counted and served by local authorities.

Unresolved: the inventory states that the bill criminalising incitement to hatred or violence on grounds including sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression passed the Chamber of Deputies on 9 January 2020, but does not record whether it was enacted, and no date of enactment is given.

Unresolved: whether the CEI 57 report approved by the Chamber of Deputies on 15 May 2025 has been implemented, or whether Circular 812 and the Gender Identity Support Program have in fact been repealed or eliminated, is not sourced. The report is described as non-binding.

Unresolved: the outcome of Isabella Panes's discrimination lawsuit against Carabineros, filed by April 2025, is not stated in the inventory.

Unresolved: the inventory gives no dates of entry into force or current legal status for the Gendarmería trans-detainee protocol, and does not indicate whether it is binding nationwide or subject to revision.

Unresolved: no source in the inventory describes document checks, gender-marker verification, or any screening procedure at ports of entry for trans visitors, so entry practice for visitors cannot be stated beyond the statutory asylum and non-discrimination provisions.

Unresolved: the F&M Global Barometers profile is cited as containing a Global Barometer of Transgender Rights index for Chile, but no score or comparison is available, so the finding is left unquantified.
